segments.say: Start from evidence rather than from a feeling. The history first, then the suite - and run the suite yourself before you ask anybody about it, because you want to know the answer before you hear an explanation of it. Three commits in the whole log: signal desk v one, the CI workflow, and a retention fix from pull request two. Read those two in that order every time. If you take the explanation first you will find yourself confirming it rather than checking it, and you will not notice that is what you are doing. And it is green. Twenty-nine tests, all passing, which is not what this lecture was going to be about. A hundred and ten milliseconds for all twenty-nine - what a suite that waits on nothing costs. Which is a good thing to have happen in front of you, because the lecture I had planned was the one where something is broken and we find it. The suite being green does not mean the repository is right.

So say so, and take the other branch. If there is no failure to diagnose, take the strongest claim in the review and ask whether it is still true - which is worth doing on any project and not just this one. A review is a snapshot. The moment anybody acts on it, half of it is stale, and there is nothing in the document that tells you which half. And read the shape of the instruction, because the shape is the transferable part. Take the claim. Check it against what is on disk right now. Say whether the review was right. Show me the evidence before you conclude anything. And do not change anything yet. That last clause is the one that keeps this honest, because an agent asked to check something and fix it will fix it, and then report that everything is fine - which is true, and useless, because you never find out what state you were actually in. Two clauses follow it on screen and both are load-bearing. Do not ask me any questions - if a choice comes up, make it and tell me what you chose and why. And: if evidence for something is missing, say it is missing rather than guessing. The first one stops a five-minute check turning into a conversation. The second is the only defence you have against a confident sentence with nothing behind it. There is a second reason to check a review rather than act on it, and it is the more important one. Everything downstream of a review inherits its mistakes silently. If the review is wrong about where a bug is, the fix pass goes to the wrong file, writes a change that makes the symptom go away, and reports success - and the only artefact of the whole misunderstanding is a diff that looks fine. And watch what counts as evidence when it comes back. Package dot json read in full, fourteen lines, with no dependencies key in it at all. ls node_modules, no such file. ls package-lock dot json, no such file. Three commands, each one re-runnable by you in ten seconds.

And what it does is the right answer. Read the verdict line, because it is doing two things at once. The claim does not hold against the current repository state - and the review was not fabricating it. Both are true. The dependency really was there, and the same commit that wrote the review also wrote the fix, so the document describes a state that existed during the build and was already gone by the time the commit landed. It goes to the file, confirms that the dependency really is gone from the package file and off the disk, and then annotates the review itself with the evidence and the date. Five lines added, one removed, at line three hundred and fourteen. The line that went said the violation exists. The five that replace it say it was found and fixed, name what is gone from disk, and stamp the date it was checked. One thing it would not close, and the refusal is the good part. The orchestrator script is still in the tools folder, sixteen kilobytes of it, deliberately left unrunnable now that its dependency is gone. It did not check whether that file still imports the package by name, and says so: a second claim, not the one I asked, so it will not assert it either way. An agent that separates what it verified from what it merely saw beats one that answers everything. So the review stops being a snapshot of this morning. It becomes a document that says what was true then, what is true now, and which of its own findings have been dealt with. Which is the small habit worth stealing from the whole lecture. When you act on a document, write the outcome back into it. Reviews, issues, plans, memory files - the ones that stay useful are the ones somebody amends, and the ones that quietly become fiction are the ones nobody ever touched again. And notice how cheap that was. One agent, read-only, two minutes, and the most valuable document in this repository is now current instead of historical. Compare that with the version of this job you have done before, which is opening a review from three weeks ago and trying to remember which parts you fixed. It is also worth noticing what it did not do, which is offer an opinion. I asked whether a specific claim was still true and it answered that question and stopped. No summary of the project's health, no list of other things it noticed, no suggestions. That is a property of the instruction rather than of the model - and it is the difference between a check you can run a hundred times and an essay you read once. If you want a tool, ask a question with a yes or a no at the end of it. And there is one more reason this beat is worth its four minutes even though nothing was broken. The next thing anybody does with this repository is read one of these documents, and the documents now disagree with each other in exactly one place fewer than they did five minutes ago.
